r2-andialbrecht__sqlparse-3512a9d86912.brief:
Stop sqlparse's `format()` from crashing on malformed SQL whose grouping goes wrong.

Today some malformed inputs make `sqlparse.format()` raise instead of returning a string. Examples: a parenthesis containing only an `AS` keyword, or only a `::` cast operator, formatted with `reindent=True` or `strip_whitespace=True`; a `CASE` with only a comma before `END`, or a `CASE ... WHEN ... THEN BEGIN ... END ELSE ... END` (where the inner `BEGIN ... END` takes the first `END`), formatted with `reindent_aligned=True`. The cause is that the generic grouping step can absorb the delimiter tokens of a group built by matching (the `(` and `)` of a parenthesis, the brackets of square brackets, the `CASE`/`END` of a case, and likewise for IF, FOR and BEGIN groups) into an inner group such as an identifier, and that the filters assume those delimiters are in place.

1. In `sqlparse/engine/grouping.py`, when `_group` is about to group a token with its previous and next tokens, refuse to do so if the previous or the next token is the first or last token (the delimiter) of the enclosing group, when that group is one of the delimited group types built by matching (parenthesis, square brackets, case, if, for, begin).
2. In the aligned-indent filter, a `CASE` without an `END` token must be handled: only align the `END` when it exists, and compute the maximum condition width with a default of 0 for an empty list.
3. In the whitespace-stripping filter, `_stripws_parenthesis` must only strip inside the brackets when the group has at least two tokens and starts with `(` and ends with `)`; otherwise fall back to the default stripping.
4. Result: `sqlparse.format()` returns a string for each of the malformed inputs above with the listed options.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

r2-andialbrecht__sqlparse-519e41698a17.brief:
Fix sqlparse's lexer so that comment and dollar-quote delimiters inside string literals or line comments no longer break the tokenization of the rest of the statement.

The earlier fix for a quadratic-time issue (GHSA-prg7-hcfm-mfcr) pairs all multiline-comment delimiters (`/*`, `/*+`, `*/`) and dollar-quote delimiters (`$$`, `$tag$`) in one pass over the raw text before lexing (`keywords.find_delimited_spans` plus `utils.resolve_paired_delimiters`). That pass does not know which offsets are inside a string literal or behind a `--` comment, so a delimiter there is paired as if it were real and consumes the partner of the next real delimiter. For example, after a string literal containing `/*` or `*/` or `/*+`, or a quoted identifier containing `/*`, or a `--` comment containing `/*`, a following real comment is mistokenized; likewise after a string or `--` comment containing a dollar delimiter, a following dollar-quoted literal is mistokenized.

1. Collect only the positions upfront: for each opener, its end offset, its tag and its token type (`Comment.Multiline.Hint` for `/*+`, `Comment.Multiline` for `/*`, `Literal` for a dollar delimiter that may open, i.e. one not preceded by a word character, `"` or `$`); for each tag, the sorted start and end offsets of its closers (all comments share the closer `*/`; every dollar delimiter can close a literal with the same tag). Return them from `find_delimited_spans(text)` as an object (`DelimitedSpans`) with an `openers` mapping and a `resolve(pos)` method that, for an opener at `pos`, finds with a binary search the first closer of the same tag starting at or after the end of the opener and returns `(end offset, token type)`, or `None` when there is none.
2. In `Lexer.get_tokens`, only when the lexer actually reaches an opener position, resolve it; if resolved, yield the whole span as one token and skip past it, otherwise continue with the normal rules. Delimiters inside strings or comments are skipped together with their surrounding token and never resolved. Unmatched openers still cost only one failed lookup each, so lexing stays linear. Remove `resolve_paired_delimiters` and its helper tuple from `sqlparse/utils.py`.
3. Find overlapping dollar delimiters too (for example with a lookahead around the delimiter pattern): in an empty dollar-quoted literal written as four dollar signs, or in a literal whose content starts with a dollar sign, the closing delimiter starts inside the text matched by the opening one, and the whole literal must still be one `Literal` token.
4. So in each example above, the real comment (or hint comment) is a single `Comment.Multiline` (or `Comment.Multiline.Hint`) token with its exact text, and the real dollar-quoted literal (also with a named tag) is a single `Literal` token with its exact text.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

r2-jfhbrook__pyee-10df5b1ce02c.brief:
Make pyee's class decorators (`pyee/cls.py`) attach to a class only the handlers that belong to that class.

Today `@on(event)` appends every decorated method to one module-level pending list, and `@evented` takes the whole list and clears it. So with nested evented classes (an inner `@evented` class defined in the body of an outer one), the inner class steals the outer class's handlers that were declared before it and the outer class loses them; and a class decorated with `evented(...)` later (not at definition time) loses its handlers to whichever class is decorated first.

1. Rename the module-level pending collection to `HANDLERS` (an instance of `Handlers`) and give `Handlers` a method `take(cls)` that removes from the pending list, and returns in their original registration order, only the handlers whose method belongs to `cls`, leaving the others pending. `evented(cls)` uses `HANDLERS.take(cls)` instead of taking everything.
2. A handler belongs to `cls` when its method object (by identity, since methods of different classes may share a name) is reachable from the values in `vars(cls)`: directly, through the function of a `staticmethod` or `classmethod`, or through a chain of `__wrapped__` attributes (as set by `functools.wraps`), possibly several levels deep. Read `__wrapped__` with `inspect.getattr_static`, so no descriptor is bound and no user-defined attribute access (such as a property named `__wrapped__`) runs. Visit each object once, so aliases and cyclic `__wrapped__` links terminate.
3. Keep everything else as it is: handler binding (a handler decorated by `@on` beneath other `functools.wraps` decorators is called without the outer wrappers; one decorated by `@on` on top of them calls through them), stacked `@on` decorators on one method and methods reachable under an alias (registration order preserved), handlers inherited from an evented parent class together with the child's own (a child's emitter calls the parent's handler then the child's), classes that create their own `event_emitter` in `__init__`, and handlers wrapped in `staticmethod` or `classmethod` (called with the instance).
4. Resulting behavior: with an inner evented class nested in an outer one, and outer handlers declared before, after or both before and after the inner class, each class's instances get exactly their own events, emitting another class's event on them reports no listener, and each handler runs on its own instance; a class decorated with `evented(...)` after another evented class was defined still gets its own handlers.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

Rework the release helper `scripts/release.py` of python-json-logger so a release tag can be moved to a corrected commit before anything is published to PyPI, without recovering artifacts from the obsolete attempt.

Today the helper reuses matching GitHub releases and assets, uploads only the files missing on PyPI (`missing_files`) and recovers earlier bundles. Replace that with a strict policy, and keep every check in plain, testable functions that raise `ValueError` with the messages below.

1. PyPI state: `pypi_files(version)` returns `None` when the version does not exist on PyPI (HTTP 404) and otherwise the mapping of published filenames to hashes. Replace `missing_files` with two checks: `require_unpublished(existing)` raises `ValueError` saying "PyPI version already exists; recover original bytes manually" for any existing record, even an empty one or a partial upload, and returns `None` when `existing` is `None`; `require_published(manifest, existing)` raises `ValueError` saying "PyPI files do not match the complete release manifest" unless `existing` equals the manifest exactly (so `None`, an empty mapping, a subset or a wrong hash all fail), and returns `None` when they match.
2. GitHub release policy: `draft_action(release, commit)` returns "create" when there is no release; raises `ValueError` saying "Published GitHub release requires owner cleanup" when the release exists and is not a draft; otherwise returns "update" when the draft's `target_commitish` equals `commit` and "replace" when it differs. Staging replaces all draft assets (recreating the draft when its commit changed) and never modifies a public release.
3. Stale runs: `require_current_commit(kind, current, expected)` raises `ValueError` saying "Release tag moved; cancel this stale run" unless the live tag resolves to an object of kind "commit" whose SHA equals the expected one; it returns `None` otherwise. A `live_tag(api)` helper resolves lightweight or annotated tags through the GitHub API and applies this check, and an `eligible(bundle, api)` check runs the tag, draft and PyPI checks before the expensive steps.
4. Bundle identity: `prepare` records `run_id` and `run_attempt` (from `GITHUB_RUN_ID` and `GITHUB_RUN_ATTEMPT`) in `release.json`. `verify_bundle(bundle)` keeps raising on a tag or commit mismatch and on a checksum mismatch as today, and additionally raises `ValueError` saying "Bundle belongs to a different workflow run" when the bundle's `run_id` differs from `GITHUB_RUN_ID`; it also requires filenames made of letters, digits and `_.+-` and SHA-256 digests of 64 lowercase hex characters, and returns the manifest when everything matches.
5. Evidence: `record_finalization(destination)` creates the directory if needed and writes `finalization.json` with exactly the keys `run_id`, `run_attempt`, `bundle_artifact_id` and `finalize`, taken from the environment variables `GITHUB_RUN_ID`, `GITHUB_RUN_ATTEMPT`, `BUNDLE_ID` and `FINALIZE`, for any outcome (success, failure or skipped).
6. Import `packaging` only inside the build/metadata commands that need it, so the publisher's preflight runs with the standard library only; the GitHub API helper must accept HTTP 204 responses (no body). Remove the old recovery and step-output helpers that are no longer used, and update the workflow and release documentation accordingly.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

r2-nhairs__python-json-logger-e76fa40928.brief:
Automate python-json-logger's releases to PyPI from version tags with a GitHub Actions workflow and a Python helper script, instead of manual builds and uploads.

Add `scripts/release.py` (Python 3.12+, run as `python scripts/release.py <command> [--bundle DIR]` with commands `prepare`, `validate`, `stage`, `recover`, `guard`, `verify`, `select`; it must also be importable as a module from its file path) and a wheel smoke-check script `scripts/release_smoke.py`, plus `.github/workflows/release.yml` and release documentation. The release policy lives in plain functions that raise `ValueError`:

1. `release_info(tag, project_version, changelog)` returns `(version, notes)`. The tag must fully match `v` followed by a `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` version whose numbers have no leading zeros, optionally followed by `.devN`, `.rcN` or `.postN` (N without leading zeros); anything else (no `v`, two components, leading zeros, `rc1` without the dot, alpha tags, extra suffixes, a trailing newline, arbitrary branch-like names) raises `ValueError`. The version is the normalised PEP 440 form (for example the rc tag gives `4.3.0rc1`, the dev and post tags keep their dotted form), and it must equal `project_version` (compared as versions), else `ValueError`. In the changelog, sections start at lines beginning with `## `; exactly one section must have a heading starting with `## [BASE]` (BASE being the `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` part) followed by `(` or whitespace, else `ValueError` (missing or duplicated section). The heading's date is the text after its last ` - `: either a real `YYYY-MM-DD` date (an invalid date such as February 30 raises) or `UNRELEASED`, which is only allowed for development releases (otherwise raise `ValueError` saying a non-development release requires a changelog date). The section body must contain at least one non-empty line that is not a heading, else `ValueError`. `notes` is the whole section (heading included) with trailing whitespace stripped and a single newline added; for a post release it is the base version's section with its original date.
2. `validate_post_date(notes, original_notes)` raises `ValueError` saying "Post release must retain the base release date" when the date in the first line of `notes` differs from the one in `original_notes`, and returns `None` otherwise. `prepare` uses it for post releases against the changelog at the base version's tag, checks that HEAD is an ancestor of `origin/main`, and writes `notes.md` and `release.json` (tag, version, commit, prerelease flag) into the bundle directory.
3. `missing_files(manifest, existing)` returns the set of manifest filenames not yet on PyPI, after checking that every existing filename is in the manifest with the same hash; otherwise it raises `ValueError` saying "PyPI files conflict with retained manifest".
4. `verify_bundle(bundle)` reads `release.json` and `SHA256SUMS.json` from the bundle directory and the files in its `dist/` subdirectory, and raises `ValueError`: "Bundle tag or commit mismatch" when the recorded tag or commit differs from `GITHUB_REF_NAME` / `GITHUB_SHA`; when the manifest does not list exactly the two files present, or not exactly one `.whl` and one `.tar.gz`; and "Invalid filename or checksum mismatch" when a name is not a plain file name or a file's SHA-256 differs from the manifest. It returns the manifest otherwise.
5. Other commands: validate that the built wheel and sdist metadata name the project and the release version and write the manifest; stage a GitHub draft release with exactly those files plus the manifest and `release.json` (reusing a matching release without modifying it, rejecting conflicting or unexpected assets); recover a missing workflow artifact from a matching official release; guard against rebuilding a partially published version; select in a read-only job the files missing on PyPI.
6. The workflow: triggered only by pushes of tags matching `v[0-9]*.[0-9]*.[0-9]*`; top-level permissions `contents: read`; job `ci` needs `validate`, `draft` needs `build`, `select` needs `draft`, `publish` needs `select`; only `draft` and `publish` get `contents: write`, and only `publish` gets `id-token: write`; every action referenced with `uses` is pinned to a 40-character commit SHA; `publish` runs in the environment named `pypi`, never checks out the repository or runs anything from `scripts/`, its second-to-last step publishes the GitHub release with `gh release edit`, and its last step uploads with `pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish`; no Python program is embedded in the workflow YAML through a here-document piped to `python -`.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

Add a cross-version summary of the complete-formatting benchmarks to python-json-logger's benchmark report tooling (`scripts/benchmark_report.py`, `scripts/benchmark_plots.py`), and collapse the detailed tables.

1. `formatting_summary(groups)` in `benchmark_report.py` takes the comparison groups produced by `comparison_groups()` (each a dict with a `python` version and `cases` keyed by `(layer, workload, series)` tuples holding a `median` in seconds) and returns, for every workload in `WORKLOADS` (in order), a dict keyed by series in the fixed order `json (CPython)`, `orjson (CPython)`, `msgspec (CPython)`, `json (PyPy)` (define this order as a module constant), containing only the series that have data. Only the `formatting` layer counts (serialization cases are ignored). Each series has up to two metrics, each with its own version coverage: `times`, built from every version that has the case, with values in microseconds (median times 1e6); and `speedup`, built only from versions that also have the `json (CPython)` formatting case of the same workload, with value reference median divided by the series' median. Each metric is a dict with `mean` (arithmetic mean of the per-version values, every version weighted equally), `min`, `max` and `versions` (the list of versions used, in group order). A metric without any value is left out (so a series measured only on a version without a CPython reference has `times` but no `speedup`), and a series with no metric is left out.

3. In the rendered report, put every Markdown table inside a collapsed admonition: before the first line of each table add a line `??? note "Timing statistics"` (when the table's header line contains `Median (µs)`) or `??? note "Speedup values"` (otherwise) followed by an empty line, and indent every table line by four spaces.
